title: AQA GCSE Physics · Moments and Pressure

items.stem: A force acts on a bar that can turn about a pivot. What is the turning effect of that force called?

options.text: The rotational force of the bar at the pivot
The leverage of the force acting on the bar
The moment of the force about the pivot
The work done by the force on the bar

items.why: The specification states that the turning effect of a force is called the moment of the force.

items.stem: The size of the moment of a force is defined by which equation?

options.text: moment of a force = weight × distance
moment of a force = force × length of bar
moment of a force = force divided by distance
moment of a force = force × distance

items.why: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it, written in symbols as M = F d.

items.stem: Which row gives the units to use in the equation M = F d?

options.text: M in newton-metres, F in grams, d in metres
M in newton-metres, F in newtons, d in metres
M in newtons, F in newtons, d in metres
M in joules, F in newtons, d in metres

items.why: These are the units the specification gives: Nm for the moment, N for the force and m for the distance.

items.stem: An object is balanced about a pivot. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment
The total of the forces on one side equals the total on the other side
Each force must act the same distance from the pivot as the other one
The pivot must be exactly at the middle of the whole object

items.why: This is the balanced condition exactly as the specification states it, about that same pivot.

items.stem: A single steady force is applied to a gate that can swing freely on its hinges. In which case does the gate rotate?

options.text: When the line of action of the force does not pass through the hinges
Only when a second force acts on the gate at the same moment
Whenever the force is larger than the weight of the gate itself
Only when the force is applied exactly at the middle of the gate

items.why: A force acting at some perpendicular distance from the pivot has a moment about it, so it turns the gate.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of a force causing an object to rotate?

options.text: A crate pulled by a rope on each side, sliding straight along the floor
Pushing on the edge of a revolving door to make it turn
Two people pushing a stalled car forwards along a flat road
A ball falling straight downwards after being dropped

items.why: The push acts at a distance from the central pivot, so it has a moment and the door rotates.

items.stem: In the equation M = F d, what exactly is the distance d?

options.text: The distance measured along the object from the pivot to where it acts
The distance the object moves in the direction of the force as it turns
The distance from one end of the object across to its far end
The perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action

items.why: This is the definition the specification gives, and it is measured in metres.

items.stem: A 60 N push is applied to a door along a line of action that passes exactly through the hinge. Why does the door not turn?

options.text: The perpendicular distance from the hinge is zero
The push is too small to overcome the weight of the door
A single force can never make a heavy object rotate
The push is applied too high up on the face of the door

items.why: With d = 0, M = F d gives a moment of zero however large the force is.

items.stem: A gardener prises up a stone using a long-handled spade as a lever. Why is a long handle better than a short one?

options.text: The longer handle increases the size of the push the gardener makes
The lever gives out more energy than the gardener puts into it
A longer handle is heavier, so it presses on the stone harder
The same push acts at a greater distance, so its moment is larger

items.why: M = F d, so increasing d while F stays the same increases the turning effect on the stone.

items.stem: What do a simple lever and a simple gear system have in common?

options.text: Both give out more energy than is put into them by the user
Both can be used to transmit the rotational effects of forces
Both increase the size of the force that you apply to them
Both change a force's direction without turning anything

items.why: This is what the specification says about them: each transmits the turning effect from one place to another.

items.stem: Two gear wheels are meshed together and the smaller one is driven clockwise. How does the larger gear turn?

options.text: Clockwise too, because the teeth push it the same way round
Anticlockwise but faster, because it is the bigger wheel
Anticlockwise, more slowly, and with a larger moment
Anticlockwise but at the same rate, because the two are joined

items.why: Meshed teeth reverse the sense; the larger wheel makes fewer turns per second and exerts a larger moment.

items.stem: A 2.0 kg bag hangs from a beam at a perpendicular distance of 0.30 m from the pivot. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the moment of the bag's weight about the pivot?

options.text: 5.9 Nm

items.why: Weight = 2.0 x 9.8 = 19.6 N, so M = F d = 19.6 x 0.30 = 5.88 Nm, which is 5.9 Nm to two significant figures.

items.stem: A force of 25 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 15 cm from a pivot. What is the moment of the force about the pivot?

options.text: 375 Nm

items.why: 15 cm = 0.15 m, so M = F d = 25 x 0.15 = 3.75 Nm, with the distance in metres as the specification requires.

items.stem: A plank balances on a pivot. A 10 N weight sits 0.60 m to the left of the pivot, and a 30 N weight sits somewhere to the right. What can be said about the 30 N weight?

options.text: It sits further from the pivot, because a larger force turns more
It sits closer to the pivot, because its force is the larger
It sits the same distance out, as the plank is balanced
It cannot balance, since the two forces are not equal

items.why: Equal moments with a larger force means a smaller distance: 0.20 m, one third of 0.60 m.

items.stem: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A 100 N weight hangs 0.75 m to the left of the pivot, and a single weight hangs 1.5 m to the right. What is that weight?
items.why: Anticlockwise moment = 100 x 0.75 = 75 Nm, so the unknown weight is 75 / 1.5 = 50 N.

items.stem: A rod is balanced on a pivot. A 6.0 N force acts 0.50 m from the pivot on one side, and an 8.0 N force acts on the other side. How far from the pivot is the 8.0 N force?
items.why: Clockwise moment = 6.0 x 0.50 = 3.0 Nm, so d = M / F = 3.0 / 8.0 = 0.375 m.

items.stem: In physics, what is meant by the term 'fluid'?

options.text: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
A liquid only, since a gas cannot be poured.
Anything that pours, such as dry sand.
A gas only, as gases fill any space.

items.why: The specification states that a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas; both can flow and both exert pressure.

items.stem: Which equation gives the pressure at the surface of a fluid?

options.text: pressure = (area of that surface)/(force normal to that surface)
pressure = (force normal to a surface) × (area of the surface)
pressure = (force parallel to a surface)/(area of that surface)
pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)

items.why: This is the equation exactly as the specification states it: p = F/A.

items.stem: In the equation p = F/A, what unit is the pressure p measured in?

options.text: Newton per metre, N/m.
Newtons, written N.
Square metres, m².
Pascals, written Pa.

items.why: The specification gives pressure, p, in pascals, Pa.

items.stem: Which word equation gives the pressure due to a column of liquid?

options.text: pressure = width of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
pressure = height of the column × area of the column × gravitational field strength
pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid / gravitational field

items.why: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it.

items.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, which units must be used for p and for h?

options.text: p in pascals, Pa and h in centimetres, cm
p in pascals, Pa and h in metres, m
p in newtons, N and h in centimetres, cm
p in newtons, N and h in metres, m

items.why: The specification gives pressure in pascals, Pa and height of the column in metres, m.

items.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, what unit must the density ρ be given in?

options.text: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.
Kilograms per litre, kg/l.
Grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³.
Newtons per metre cubed, N/m³.

items.why: The specification gives density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.

items.stem: An exam question asks for the pressure at the bottom of a column of sea water. What does the specification say about the gravitational field strength g?

options.text: It must be recalled from memory as 9.8 N/kg.
It is measured in newtons, N, and is recalled.
It is always taken as exactly 10 N/kg here.
Its value will be given in the question, in N/kg.

items.why: The specification states that in any calculation the value of g will be given.

items.stem: A submerged object experiences a greater pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface. What is the resultant upward force called?

options.text: The force by which upthrust beats weight.
The upthrust on the object.
A normal contact force from the water below.
The water's push under its base only.

items.why: The specification names this resultant upward force the upthrust.

items.stem: Which statement best describes a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere?

options.text: A deep layer of gas that gets denser as altitude rises.
A thick layer of air of the same density at all heights.
A layer of air about as deep as the Earth is wide.
A thin layer of air round the Earth that thins with altitude.

items.why: The specification describes a thin layer, relative to the size of the Earth, that gets less dense with altitude.

items.stem: A sealed can holds compressed air. In which direction does the air pressure exert a force on the flat top of the can?

options.text: Vertically downwards, pulled by the air's weight.
At right angles to the top, pushing outwards.
Sideways across the top, following the airflow.
Inwards to the centre of the sealed can.

items.why: The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface it touches.

items.stem: Water in a reservoir presses on a sloping side wall. How does the force from the water act on that wall?

options.text: Vertically downwards all the way down the wall.
Straight downwards, in line with the water's weight.
Normal to the wall at every point along it.
Along the wall, the way the water runs.

items.why: Pressure in a fluid causes a force at right angles to the surface, whatever its angle.

items.stem: Explain why the pressure at a point in a liquid increases as that point gets deeper.

options.text: The liquid becomes denser lower down, where it is squashed.
The liquid flows downwards, pressing harder low down.
A taller column of liquid lies above it, weighing more.
The container holds a lot more liquid low down than high up.

items.why: Pressure is h ρ g: a greater height of liquid above the point means more weight above it.

items.stem: Two tanks are filled to the same depth, one with water and one with mercury. Why is the pressure at the base greater in the mercury?

options.text: Mercury is denser, so the column above weighs more.
The mercury must be filled to a greater depth.
Mercury is denser, so its column is taller than water.
Mercury fills up more volume at the same depth here.

items.why: In p = h ρ g the height is the same, so the greater density gives the greater pressure.

items.stem: A sealed can is held completely under water. Why does the water exert a resultant upward force on it?

options.text: Water pushes up on the bottom and not down on the top.
The can is full of air, which is lighter than the water.
Only the bottom face has water pushing on it.
Pressure on its bottom face exceeds that on its top.

items.why: The bottom face is deeper, so the pressure there is greater and the resultant force is upwards.

items.stem: A solid block is lowered into a tank of water and floats. Which statement explains why it floats?

options.text: Its density is lower than the density of the water.
It is lighter than water, whatever its size or shape.
The upthrust on it is larger than its own weight.
It has a large volume and holds a lot of air.

items.why: Floating and sinking are decided by comparing the density of the object with that of the liquid.

items.stem: Explain why atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain is lower than at sea level.

options.text: Gravity is much weaker at the top of a high mountain.
The air up there is colder, so it presses down less hard.
There is less air above, so fewer molecules collide.
The wind is stronger high up, blowing the air away.

items.why: Fewer air molecules above the surface means less weight of air and fewer collisions with it.

items.stem: A force of 4500 N acts at right angles to a surface of area 0.03 m². Calculate the pressure on the surface.

options.text: 135 Pa

items.stem: A crate presses on the floor with a force of 2400 N normal to the floor and exerts a pressure of 800 Pa. Calculate the area of contact.

options.text: 3 m²
30 m²

items.stem: A force of 16 N acts normal to a surface of area 200 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals. 1 m² = 10 000 cm²

options.text: 8 Pa
80 Pa
800 Pa

items.stem: A brick of mass 2.0 kg rests flat on a bench. gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Which value is the force normal to the bench in p = F/A?

options.text: 19.6 N, the weight of the brick.
2.0 N, the mass rewritten in newtons.
9.8 N, the field strength in N/kg.
0.20 N, the mass divided by g.

items.why: F must be a force in newtons: weight = 2.0 x 9.8 = 19.6 N.

items.stem: A walker on soft snow puts on wide snowshoes and stops sinking in. Why?

options.text: The larger area increases the pressure on the snow.
The larger area reduces the pressure on the snow.
The larger area presses down harder on the snow.
The force is the walker's mass, and wide shoes shrink it.

items.why: The normal force is unchanged but is spread over more area, so p = F/A falls.

items.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, how is the height h of the liquid column found from the other quantities?

options.text: Multiply the pressure by ρ g.
Divide ρ g by the pressure value.
Subtract ρ g from the pressure.
Divide the pressure by ρ g.

items.why: ρ and g multiply h in p = h ρ g, so h = p divided by ρ g.

items.stem: Calculate the pressure due to a column of water of height 25 m. density of water = 1000 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

options.text: 245 Pa

items.stem: A diver swims from a depth of 8.0 m to a depth of 12.0 m. density of sea water = 1030 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Calculate the increase in pressure on the diver.

options.text: 420 Pa
